passages.t: Praise from her feet to her head
passages.happening:
The man praises the woman again, this time from her feet upward. ‘How beautiful are your sandaled feet, O daughter of the prince’ (verse 1), he begins, and he moves upward in pictures of jewels, wine, wheat ringed with lilies and fawns (verses 1-3).

‘Your neck is like a tower made of ivory; your eyes are like the pools of Heshbon by the gate of Bath-rabbim; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, facing toward Damascus’ (verse 4). ‘Your head crowns you like Mount Carmel, the hair of your head like purple threads; the king is captured in your tresses’ (verse 5).

‘How fair and pleasant you are, O love, with your delights’ (verse 6). He pictures her as a tall palm tree, and himself as longing to climb it and take hold of its fruit, and he asks that her kiss be like the finest wine (verses 7-9).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 6 closed with a call for the Shulammite to turn so that others could see her. Chapter 7 is the longest and boldest description of her in the book. Earlier the man praised her from the head downward (4:1-7), and she praised him the same way (5:10-16). Here the gaze moves from her feet upward. The friction and searching of chapters 5 and 6 are past, and their love is at its most confident.

Poems that praise a lover part by part are known from across the ancient world, and scholars often call them by the Arabic word wasf. The comparisons are not pictures in the modern sense. A neck like an ivory tower suggests grace and worth; eyes like pools suggest depth and calm; a nose like the tower of Lebanon suggests dignity, not size. Wheat, wine, palm fruit and vines belong to a farming world where harvest meant life and celebration.

The places span the land and its borders. Heshbon was a city east of the Jordan, once the capital of the Amorite king Sihon, and Bath-rabbim may be one of its gates. The tower of Lebanon facing Damascus points north. Carmel is the ridge that rises over the Mediterranean. Purple was a costly dye made from sea snails, linked with royalty. The poet wants her beauty to fill the whole land.
passages.later: Heshbon was the city of Sihon king of the Amorites (Numbers 21:26). And the Bible honors the love the chapter celebrates: Proverbs urges a husband to ‘rejoice in the wife of your youth’ (Proverbs 5:18).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible contain such frank physical imagery, and how should a reader handle it?

Some readers are embarrassed by a chapter like this, and through history many preferred to read it only as allegory, so as to avoid its plain sense.

But the Bible does not treat physical love as dirty. Genesis presents man and woman as made for each other and naked without shame (Genesis 2:25). Proverbs urges a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth (Proverbs 5:18-19). Paul tells married couples not to deprive each other (1 Corinthians 7:3-5). The Song gives voice to that goodness in poetry, and its language is veiled and full of images, not graphic.

Most interpreters, including those who read it as a courtship, read it within the Bible's wider frame, where sexual love belongs to the covenant of marriage, and the book's own refrain warns against awakening love before its time (2:7; 3:5; 8:4).

Readers who find the chapter uncomfortable are right to handle it with reverence. But reverence here means receiving the gift, not hiding from it.
passages.asks: He sees her beauty filling the whole land. If you are married, ask whether you still see your husband or wife with that kind of wonder. And ask how you can speak of the body, your own and others', with the reverence this chapter shows.

passages.t: Desire turned toward her, and a walk to the fields
passages.happening:
She answers with the fullest form of the Song's refrain of belonging: “I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me” (verse 10).

Then she takes the lead. ‘Come, my beloved, let us go to the countryside; let us spend the night among the wildflowers’ (verse 11). They will go early to the vineyards to see if the vines have budded and the pomegranates bloomed, and there she will give him her love (verse 12). ‘The mandrakes send forth a fragrance, and at our door is every delicacy, new as well as old, that I have treasured up for you, my beloved’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Verse 10 is the third and fullest statement of belonging (compare 2:16 and 6:3). This time she does not say he is hers, but that his desire is for her. Desire is teshuqah, a rare word found only three times in the Hebrew Bible: here, in Genesis 3:16, where after the fall the woman's desire is for her husband and he rules over her, and in Genesis 4:7. Many readers hear in verse 10 a reversal of Genesis 3:16. Here desire runs toward her, and no one rules.

Verses 11 to 13 echo the spring invitation of 2:10-13, but now she is the one inviting. The garden that in chapter 4 was a picture of her becomes a place they go together.

Mandrakes were a plant with a strong scent and a forked root, which ancient people linked with love and fertility. The Hebrew word for mandrakes sounds like the word for love, a play the poet surely meant.
passages.later: The same rare word for desire stands in Genesis, after the fall: ‘Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you’ (Genesis 3:16). And Rachel and Leah once bargained over mandrakes (Genesis 30:14-16).
passages.asks: She says, with confidence, that his desire is for her. Ask whether the love in your life, given and received, is free of rule and fear. And ask what it would mean to invite someone you love away, simply to be together.
